Central Bank Regulatory Dynamic & Operational Milestone
Direct Impact on Financial Inclusion & Household Liquidity
2014 - Pre-Escalation Baseline
Unified Central Bank of Yemen (CBY) in Sana'a; stable managed peg at 215 YER/USD backed by oil export revenues and reserves (~$4.5B).
Full national clearing of cheques; uniform banknote acceptability; basic credit markets functioning.
2015 - Conflict Outbreak & Blockade
Oil exports halt; foreign exchange reserves deplete rapidly; CBY begins rationing import letters of credit.
Initial cash withdrawal limits imposed by commercial banks; public deposits begin drying up.
2016 - CBY Relocation to Aden (Sept 2016)
Presidential decree relocates formal CBY headquarters to Aden; Sana'a establishes de facto central bank administration. Public salaries stop.
Severance of sovereign clearing system; commercial banks caught between contradictory regulatory directives.
2017 - New Banknote Printing (Aden)
CBY-Aden contracts Russian Goznak to print new banknote issues (different size/design) to address acute physical liquidity deficit.
New banknotes enter circulation in southern and eastern governorates; accepted initially nationwide.
2019 - Northern Banknote Ban (Dec 2019)
CBY-Sana'a strictly bans the circulation of newly printed Aden banknotes in northern territories, criminalizing possession.
Beginning of monetary bifurcation; old banknotes in north trade at premium; birth of internal remittance exchange fees.
2021 - Escalating Divergence & Float
CBY-Aden increases money supply printing; currency depreciates past 1,000 YER/USD. Sana'a fixes rate via strict security enforcement.
Hawala transfer fee from Aden to Sana'a surges to 55-60% of principal, imposing crushing transaction costs on domestic remittances.
2022 - Findex Survey Round (Late 2022)
Saudi/UAE $2B deposit announced; temporary stabilization of southern currency. Northern banknotes suffer extreme physical wear.
Findex survey captures acute household liquidity exhaustion; formal banking completely bypassed for cross-line commerce.
2024 - Heightened Central Bank Confrontation
CBY-Aden mandates relocation of bank HQs from Sana'a to Aden; revokes licenses of non-compliant banks. Sana'a issues new 100 YER coin.
SWIFT access severed for non-compliant banks; internal remittance commission exceeds 70%; commercial payments face paralysis.
2026 - Current Structural State
Two entirely distinct monetary systems operate within one country: inflationary floating regime (South) vs. fixed repressed regime (North).
Digital wallets and money exchangers function as de facto central clearinghouses, absorbing all cross-territory friction.

Emergency Cash Transfer Project (ECTP)
UNICEF / World Bank (IDA) / SFD
~1.5 million vulnerable households (~9 million individuals) from the Social Welfare Fund (SWF) caseload.
Unconditional physical cash in local currency delivered at fixed temporary payment sites.
Microfinance Banks (Al-Amal Microfinance Bank, Al-Kuraimi Islamic Bank) and accredited money exchange sub-agents.
Strict face-to-face photo verification against SWF baseline list, biometric verification pilot, third-party monitoring.
High logistics cost transporting physical cash to remote mountainous areas; acute currency exchange rate volatility.
High potential to transition beneficiaries into permanent mobile wallets, but constrained by lack of smartphones and low digital literacy.
General Food Assistance (GFA) Cash/Voucher
World Food Programme (WFP)
~13 million food-insecure individuals (mix of in-kind food, commodity vouchers, and cash transfers).
Combination of paper commodity vouchers, Scope electronic smartcards, and direct cash disbursements.
Retail trader networks, contracted money exchangers, and selected microfinance bank branch counters.
WFP Scope biometric iris/fingerprint scanning; facing severe regulatory suspension in northern governorates since 2019.
Food price inflation rapidly erodes purchasing power of cash allowances; supplier cash-out liquidity caps.
Scope card acts as closed-loop store-value instrument; could be upgraded to open-loop interoperable debit card.
Social Fund for Development (SFD) Cash-for-Work
SFD / World Bank / UNDP / FCDO
~200,000 extreme-poor rural youth and household heads engaged in community infrastructure rehabilitation.
Conditional cash wage transfers paid in monthly tranches upon completion of public infrastructure work.
Al-Amal Bank (PYes wallet), Kuraimi Bank, and local hawala exchange agents.
National ID verification, community oversight committees, and GPS-tagged work attendance logs.
Security checkpoints delay cash armored vehicles; discrepancy in banknote denominations across frontlines.
Directly catalyzes digital inclusion: participants are required to open digital mobile wallets to receive wage tranches.
Rapid Response Mechanism (RRM)
UNFPA / IOM / UNICEF / WFP
Newly displaced IDP families fleeing active frontlines, floods, or natural hazards (~500,000 individuals annually).
One-off multi-purpose cash assistance (MPCA) delivered within 72 hours of sudden displacement.
Mobile money transfer codes sent via SMS or redeemable at any local money exchange counter.
Immediate biometric/ID verification bypassed in favor of localized displacement certificates and community focal points.
Lost identification documents prevent formal banking onboarding; complete reliance on agent OTC cash payouts.
Low initial inclusion; serves as emergency humanitarian survival rail; graduation requires post-displacement civil re-registration.

Commercial Banks (Conventional & Islamic)
Severely divided between Central Bank of Yemen (CBY) Aden and CBY Sana'a; conflicting regulatory circulars, compliance directives, and dual exchange rates.
Heavily contracted; branches restricted to tier-1 cities (Sana'a, Aden, Taiz, Hodeidah, Mukalla). Rural physical presence is negligible (<5% of branches).
Rigid Tier-1 KYC: Requires physical biometric national ID, utility bill proof of residence, salary certificates, and corporate references. Extremely high barrier for IDPs and informal workers.
Severely damaged by historical deposit lockups, acute cash liquidity shortages, limits on foreign currency withdrawals, and asset impairment from government debt defaults.
Fragmented interbank clearing; traditional SWIFT links disrupted for many northern banks; de facto reliance on physical cash transfers or cross-border clearing via correspondent banks in GCC.
Handle large institutional and corporate wires, oil import financing, and formal multilateral funding tranches, but largely bypassed by retail consumers.
Need regulatory unification, tiered e-KYC regulations, digital onboarding sandboxes, and restructuring of legacy non-performing sovereign exposures.
Microfinance Banks (MFBs - e.g. Kuraimi, Al-Amal, Tadhamon MFI)
Regulated under dedicated Microfinance Laws; actively operate across conflict frontlines under pragmatic operational compromises to preserve nationwide remittance corridors.
Extensive hybrid branch and agency network penetrating secondary towns, market centers, and peri-urban hubs. Better liquidity management than commercial peers.
Adapted Tier-2 KYC: Permits recognized local identity cards, family cards, or community leader certifications for low-balance accounts.
High consumer trust; perceived as resilient, accessible, and community-embedded institutions that kept teller windows open during peak conflict periods.
Operate proprietary payment switches (e.g. Kuraimi Express); partially integrated with mobile network operator wallet platforms.
Primary disbursement channel for humanitarian cash assistance programs (Unicef ECTP, WFP, Social Fund for Development / SFD transfers).
Catalyze digital micro-credit, micro-savings, and solar/agricultural productive financing via digital wallet interfaces.
Mobile Money Wallets (e.g. Floosak, mFloos, Jawali, Weyak)
Subject to evolving mobile payment guidelines; hindered by fragmented licensing between Aden and Sana'a authorities and telecom regulatory disputes (4G/telecom licensing).
Leverages existing telecom agents, grocers, and money exchange cash-in/cash-out points. Reaches areas without formal brick-and-mortar bank branches.
Simplified Tier-3 KYC: Onboarding via mobile phone number, digital national ID photo, or agent verification. Minimal friction but subject to low transaction/balance ceilings.
Growing adoption among tech-savvy youth and merchants; lingering skepticism among older adults regarding non-cash stored value security.
Limited national interoperability; historically siloed closed-loop networks, though Unified Payment Network (UPN) initiatives in Aden aim to enable cross-wallet clearing.
Rapidly expanding in retail merchant checkout, private solar utility subscriptions, mobile top-ups, and peer-to-peer (P2P) transfers.
Mandate standardized QR interoperability, zero-rate cash-in/cash-out merchant fees, and integrate with civil servant payroll and UN e-vouchers.
Money Exchange Companies (MECs / Hawala Brokers)
Dominant financial intermediaries; licensed by CBY but historically operating with high autonomy; intensive regulatory clampdowns by CBY-Aden to curb FX speculation.
Massive, highly agile physical footprint extending to almost every rural village and district market; superior liquidity logistics capable of transporting cash across governorates.
Variable KYC: Ranges from formal ledger recording of ID to informal kinship recognition (Hawala trust mechanism). Highly susceptible to AML/CFT compliance challenges.
Highest retail trust and daily operational reliance; public views MECs as reliable, instantaneous cash remittance conduits without balance freeze risks.
Operate private, proprietary hawala clearing networks; settle net balances via physical cash shipments, commercial bank accounts, or cross-border trade netting.
Facilitate over 80% of personal domestic remittances, international diaspora inflows (~$4-5 billion annually), and last-mile humanitarian cash distributions.
Formalize as licensed micro-banking agents, enforce digital reporting and AML/CFT compliance, and channel hawala liquidity into formal digital accounts.
